learn.title: A pointer is an address in a variable
learn.body: You learned that `&n` is the address of `n`. A pointer is a variable that stores such an address. Instead of holding a number like 7, it holds the location of a number. Pointers let code reach data that lives somewhere else.

learn.title: The declaration
learn.body: `int *p;` declares `p` as a pointer to an `int`. Read the star as "pointer to". To make `p` point at `n`, store its address: `int *p = &n;`. The type matters: an `int *` is meant to point at an `int`, a `char *` at a `char`.

learn.title: Comparing p and &n
learn.body: This prints 1, then 8. The first line is 1 (true) because `p` holds exactly the address `&n`. A pointer takes 8 bytes on the 64-bit platforms we use, whatever it points to.

learn.title: Reading declarations
steps: `int *p;` means p is a pointer to int
`char *s;` means s is a pointer to char
`double *d;` means d is a pointer to double
All of them are 8 bytes here: just an address

learn.body: Careful with commas: `int *a, b;` makes `a` a pointer but `b` a plain `int`. Write one declaration per line to avoid surprises.

questions.prompt: `int *p;` declares p as a \_\_ to an int.
questions.explanation: The star in a declaration means pointer to.

questions.prompt: What does a pointer variable store?
questions.explanation: A pointer stores the address of another value.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does a pointer take on a 64-bit platform?
questions.explanation: An address on these platforms is 64 bits, which is 8 bytes.

questions.prompt: Which line declares a pointer to a `char`?
questions.explanation: The type comes first, then the star, then the name.

questions.prompt: In `int *a, b;` which of these is a pointer?
questions.explanation: The star belongs to the name `a`. `b` is a plain `int`.
`p` was set to the address of `n`, so they are equal.

questions.prompt: Match each declaration to what it declares.
questions.explanation: A star after the type marks a pointer.
